newsitem.title: UK: Plymouth pundits enter UK election spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Plymouth pundits enter UK election spotlight.

text.p: As Britain's six-week election campaign enters the home stretch, many bored electors have already switched off their television sets.
But for the die-hard armchair viewer, two political pundits are now familiar faces after their role in the campaign.

They may lack the clout of John Major and Tony Blair, but Colin Rallings and Michael Thrasher's expertise in voting behaviour and analysis of the issues explains the political state of play to the television-watching public.
Rallings and Thrasher are psephologists, the tongue-twisting tag for someone who studies elections. Both are professors of politics at the University of Plymouth.
Whenever an election -- local, national or European -- occurs, they step from the academic world to the bright lights of television.

The pair have been described as "the Starsky and Hutch of psephology". But they're not overly keen on that image and stress that both sides of their work -- academic research and television appearances -- are of equal importance.
Rallings works for Independent Television News (ITN) while Thrasher has signed up with Rupert Murdoch's Sky News. Both take part in Reuters polls of opinion on the outcome of the election.
Providing an alternative to public opinion polls, Rallings and Thrasher measure political party support by analysing results of local and by-elections.
Unlike most polls, they never believed Neil Kinnock's Labour party would win in 1992, but neither think there will be a last-minute reprieve for John Major's Conservative party.
In a Reuters poll published on Wednesday, Rallings predicted an 81-seat majority for Labour and a lead of nine percentage points. Thrasher put Labour's majority at 65 seats with a nine-point lead.
The task of predicting human behaviour is virtually impossible and the pair admit having differences of opinion.
"To be honest with you...we probably own between us two or three different predictions of what is going to happen," admits Rallings. Thrasher nods in agreement.

They have been academic colleagues since the late 1970s, but it was not until 1984 when the Local Government Chronicle (LGC) -- a magazine for professionals in local government -- first published one of their articles that they collaborated.
"We've written a piece every month since July 1984," Thrasher says.
"At least once a month without a break. It frightens me sometimes," Rallings chips in.

Processing, analysing and publishing local election results is a huge task. "The work we do is too extensive and too time-consuming for anybody to do it on their own and it really does become a joint project," Rallings says.
In today's world where the "soundbite" is all-important, their task is to distil complex research, combine it with the issues of the day, and convey the message in a snappy way.
"ITN is about trying to pack things into as short a space as possible. I've become quite good, I think, at saying what I have to say in 20 or even 10 seconds," Rallings said.
Thrasher has a little more time. At the 1992 election he was in Sky's studio from nine in the evening until 5.30 the following morning.

Both enjoy television work and have learnt to "sell" their opinions. Describing Labour's massive lead of between 14 and 19 points in most recent opinion polls, Thrasher said: "Labour's got a three-nil lead with ten minutes to go. All it needs to do is keep possession."
